book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer

chapters.file: ch05 - Part IV The Simpsons and the Philosophers.md
chapters.relation: Six essays apply named philosophers to the show. James Lawler reads each Simpson through Kantian duty versus desire: Homer's mental 'Marge' approvingly rationalizes wrecking Moe's car in 'Dumbell Indemnity,' Marge risks her realty career in 'Realty Bites' rather than conceal the murder house from the Flanders family, and Lisa's vegetarianism in 'Lisa the Vegetarian' tests whether her maxims can be universalized. Paul Cantor argues the show paradoxically defends the nuclear family against both the therapeutic foster-care state ('Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily') and Flanders-style piety, and reads the Mensa junta of 'They Saved Lisa's Brain' as a failed Platonic rule of philosopher-kings toppled by Homer's counterrevolution of the stupid. Jason Holt uses Chief Wiggum's open bribes to argue hypocrisy need not involve deception; Daniel Barwick blames Mr. Burns's unhappiness on seeing everything (bowling trophies, Schindler comparisons, 'iced cream') as mere symbol, an infinite regress of instrumental without intrinsic goodness; David Vessey justifies Flanders baptizing the Simpson children through Kantian autonomy, so 'love your neighbor as yourself' does not require saving autonomous agents from their own principled choices; Jennifer McMahon extends Martha Nussbaum's case that fiction morally educates, arguing The Simpsons' ordinariness, comedy, animation, and mass appeal make it a heuristic fiction.

Three essays plus the start of the episode list. James Wallace's Marxist reading argues that although The Simpsons' incongruity-based jokes (Homer offering his family to aliens, telling Apu he'll 'really, really miss' him after scapegoating him in 'Much Apu About Nothing') momentarily distance us from capitalist ideology, episodes like 'Scenes from the Class Struggle in Springfield' end by restoring the social order, so the show subverts its own subversion and laughter becomes an opiate. David Arnold applies Barthes's Mythologies, 'Rhetoric of the Image,' and S/Z to 'The Front,' treating Bart and Lisa's Itchy & Scratchy script and the Elvis impersonator shooting his TV as a writerly text of free-floating signifiers that resists closed reading. Kelly Dean Jolley contrasts Schopenhauer's 'world is my idea' with Heidegger's tree in bloom and Frege's anti-psychologism, casting Bart as a Heideggerian thinker whose thoughts are not in his head but out among beings, face-to-face with the world.

holes.name: Semiotics (signifier and signified)
holes.what: Barthes's semiological method (via Saussure) that analyzes cultural signs into signifier and signified, denotation and connotation, and distinguishes readerly from writerly texts.
holes.why: Chapter 6's essay on 'The Front' is built entirely on Barthesian semiotics and the readerly/writerly distinction, and no taxonomy concept covers signifier/signified analysis.

holes.name: Anti-Psychologism
holes.what: Frege's doctrine (radicalized by Heidegger) that thoughts and logic are not private psychological events in the head but sharable items outside individual minds.
holes.why: Chapter 6's 'What Bart Calls Thinking' turns on the Frege-Heidegger fight against psychologism to present Bart's thoughts as out in the world, and no existing concept captures this doctrine.

holes.name: Intrinsic vs Instrumental Goodness
holes.what: The distinction between things good in themselves and things good only as means to further goods, with the regress problem that purely instrumental value is never grounded.
holes.why: Chapter 5's Mr. Burns essay argues his representationalism leaves only instrumental value with nothing intrinsically good, which is why nothing in his life can be meaningful or happy.
